title: Error analysis and controlled follow-up
goals: Design a controlled change with a stated hypothesis

prerequisite.prompt: What does a confusion matrix omit?
prerequisite.answer: It counts outcome combinations but does not explain the causes of individual errors.

vocabulary: Inspection of mistakes to propose explanations
A comparison that changes one planned factor while holding relevant conditions fixed
A new failure introduced by a change

blocks.text: Error analysis begins with prediction IDs and reference labels. Inspect features, collection conditions and the labelling policy. Do not assume every surprising prediction proves the reference is wrong. Use development errors to propose a change and specify what outcome would support the explanation.

Use fictional classroom data throughout this investigation. Keep the task, units, reference labels and data split visible as you reason. Earlier weeks supplied the model-building process; this week examines error analysis and controlled follow-up.

A validation audit has 12 dim-light cases with 4 errors and 18 bright-light cases with 3 errors. Rates are 4/12=1/3 and 3/18=1/6. Dim lighting is a useful lead, not proof of causation: camera, route or labels may also differ. A planned change uses a training-fitted brightness normalization while keeping split and classifier settings fixed.

blocks.title: Python 3 check
blocks.text:
old_errors = [4, 3]
new_errors = [2, 4]
counts = [12, 18]
for old, new, n in zip(old_errors, new_errors, counts):
    print(old / n, new / n)
print(sum(old_errors), sum(new_errors))
# Total errors fall from 7 to 6; one group worsens.

Trace the calculation on paper before running this optional Python check. Use the stated fictional inputs and compare intermediate values. The code checks this example; your independent workbook case uses different evidence.

blocks.title: Error analysis and controlled follow-up at a glance
blocks.caption: After the change, the same validation groups have 2/12 and 4/18 errors. Total errors fall from 7 to 6, but bright-light errors increase from 3 to 4. Report both results. A net improvement does not mean every part improved, and repeated experiments can overfit validation.

blocks.label: Does the difference prove dim light causes model errors? Explain the steps or evidence behind your response.

blocks.text: Write a change record: hypothesis, exact code/data version, controlled factors, predicted effect, full before/after results and decision. Review disagreements using a consistent annotation policy. If labels are corrected, version the data and rerun all candidates on the same corrected evaluation set.

Do not delete difficult cases to raise the score or reuse final-test errors for an unreported revision. Once test feedback guides a change, treat it as development evidence and obtain a new independent evaluation for a fresh final claim.

blocks.label: A team removes all disputed records only from the new model report. Why is the comparison invalid?

workbook.title: Find the rates
workbook.prompt: Calculate the original error rates by lighting condition.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Dim 4/12 about 33.3 percent; bright 3/18 about 16.7 percent.

workbook.title: Explain the limit
workbook.prompt: Does the difference prove dim light causes model errors?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: No. Other conditions and label quality may differ; it motivates a hypothesis.

workbook.title: Track regressions
workbook.prompt: Summarize the changed results without hiding a regression.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Total errors 7 to 6; dim 4 to 2 improves, bright 3 to 4 worsens.

workbook.title: Apply independently
workbook.prompt: Old errors are 5/10 on route A and 2/20 on B. New errors are 3/10 and 5/20. State total and group changes and a justified next step.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Total worsens 7/30 to 8/30. A improves 50 to 30 percent, B worsens 10 to 25 percent. Investigate B and keep the original as a comparison; do not claim overall improvement.

workbook.title: Repair a misleading audit
workbook.prompt: A team removes all disputed records only from the new model report. Why is the comparison invalid?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: The models are evaluated on different selected records. Apply one documented review policy and compare both on the same versioned set.

teacher.background: Teach two 45-minute sessions. This week focuses on error analysis and controlled follow-up. Model the worked example first, collect the new W 4 case independently before feedback, and use the fresh retry to check transfer. Award credit for traceable reasoning and bounded claims, including justified uncertainty.
materials: Paper, pencils and a calculator for fractions
The fictional examples and a blank evidence table
Optional Python 3 editor; no external packages or AI accounts required
sessions: Use the prerequisite question: What does a confusion matrix omit? Check the explanation before proceeding.
Read the opening and model the worked evidence. Ask students to identify error analysis in context.
Complete W 1 and W 2 with support: find the rates; explain the limit. Require the evidence, not only the final response.
Read the visual row by row. Collect the guided explanation and compare reasoning in pairs. Trace the Python check after the paper calculation.
Retrieve the distinction between error analysis and hypothesis. Invite a counterexample to an overconfident claim.
Discuss the application and complete W 3: Summarize the changed results without hiding a regression.
Collect W4 independently before giving hints. Assess these outcomes: Categorize development errors using evidence; Design a controlled change with a stated hypothesis. Record any support used.
Use W 5 and the exit response to assess limits. Give targeted feedback, then the fresh retry. Save evidence of independent understanding.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided response: No. Other conditions and label quality may differ; it motivates a hypothesis. Exit response: The models are evaluated on different selected records. Apply one documented review policy and compare both on the same versioned set.
misconceptions: Ask for the relevant counts, units, procedure or saved record. For this week: Dim 4/12 about 33.3 percent; bright 3/18 about 16.7 percent.
A stronger claim makes a stronger project
The models are evaluated on different selected records. Apply one documented review policy and compare both on the same versioned set.
The new case can be copied from the example

The independent task changes the evidence. Require a fresh explanation: Total worsens 7/30 to 8/30. A improves 50 to 30 percent, B worsens 10 to 25 percent. Investigate B and keep the original as a comparison; do not claim overall improvement.
teacher.assessment: For independent W 4, require: Total worsens 7/30 to 8/30. A improves 50 to 30 percent, B worsens 10 to 25 percent. Investigate B and keep the original as a comparison; do not claim overall improvement. Fresh retry: old groups 2/8 and 4/12; new 3/8 and 2/12. Total improves 6/20 to 5/20 while the first group regresses. Require both statements. Mark each criterion as independent, supported or not yet demonstrated. Reassess the reasoning after feedback; do not replace the first attempt silently.
teacher.support: Provide a blank evidence table and allow a verbal explanation before writing. Highlight the given conditions without supplying the W 4 conclusion. Use error analysis and hypothesis in full sentences. Extension: alter one condition in the worked example and explain which conclusion changes and which remains supported.
teacher.next: Next week: Regression and residuals. Carry forward the saved evidence and the distinction between development choices and justified claims.
